correctness.rationale: The inequality \(\tau(n)\le2^{\Omega(n)}\) restricts \(\tau(n)\) below \(256\) to the perfect values \(6\) or \(28\). Fresh partition enumeration confirms that \(\tau=6\) gives exponent patterns \((5)\) or \((2,1)\), while the only \(\Omega=8\) pattern with perfect divisor count is \((6,1,1)\) and \(\tau=28\). The \(p^5\) shape is impossible because \(\sigma(p^5)\) has at least two distinct odd prime factors. The \(p^2q\) shape forces \(p^2+p+1=2^s-1\) and \(q=2^{s-1}-1\); simultaneous primality gives \(s=3\), then only \(p=2\), contradicting oddness. For \((6,1,1)\), Euclid--Euler forces the exact Mersenne/cyclotomic equations, and the modulo-eight calculation forces \(p\equiv1\pmod8\). The converse is immediate by multiplying divisor-sum factors.
correctness.risk: The theorem does not prove that the equality-layer Diophantine system has a solution.

originality.rationale: Brown derives a general Mersenne-based form for odd sublime numbers only under the explicit assumption that no odd perfect numbers exist. At low multiplicity the audited argument removes that global assumption because \(\tau(n)<256\) forces the relevant perfect divisor counts to be the even perfect numbers \(6\) and \(28\), and it then completely excludes the \(\Omega<8\) shapes. Brown's conditional template anticipates the equality-layer architecture, so the originality is the unconditional low-layer closure rather than discovery of the Mersenne mechanism itself. OEIS contains a 2025 comment claiming all sublime numbers have a Mersenne form but supplies no proof or covering reference; MathWorld still states that existence of odd sublime numbers is unknown.

final_claim: Every odd sublime number satisfies \(\Omega(n)\ge8\); at \(\Omega(n)=8\), the odd sublime numbers are exactly the integers \(p^6(2^a-1)(2^b-1)\) satisfying the stated distinct-prime, Mersenne-prime, cyclotomic equation \(\Phi_7(p)=2^{a+b+1}-1\), with \(a,b\) distinct odd primes and \(p\equiv1\pmod8\).
